title: Phrases a shooter needs on the stand
summary: Short English phrases for the coach, the referee and your squad: what to say and when, and where a polite question ends and pressure on the referee begins.

body.html: On the stand you mostly listen. Still, a few short phrases help a lot: to tell the coach what you saw, to deal with the referee correctly and to be polite to your squad. What the referee says is in What the referee says on the stand.

After a miss, the coach needs your picture (what you saw at the shot). Say where you saw the target and where you think the shot went: “I saw it late”, “I think I was behind”, “I lost it in the trees”. If you are not sure, say so. “I don’t know” is useful information too.
Ask for what you need. In training you can ask to see the target again, to go a little slower, or for the coach to show the line with his hands. Ask while your gun is open, not during your routine.

With the referee, the rules give you very few words. The call is a short, clear “Pull!” or “Ready!”, said the same way each time. The target must then come within 3 seconds; if it comes later, the referee calls a No Bird.

html.sporting: Raise a hand at once, on the stand, and say “Protest!” or “Appeal!”. Once you call for the next target, the rules treat that as accepting the decision, so protest before you call again.
html.compak: Raise an arm at once, before the next shooter calls, and say “Protest!” or “Appeal!”. Then give your reason.

body.html: After a protest, say briefly why: “I saw a piece come off” (a visible piece makes a hit) or “It came late”. Then accept the answer. If the referee is sure, the decision stands and is final. The full procedure, including the appeal to the jury, is in Results, protests and appeals.

Calm, short questions are normal: “Was that a No Bird?” or “Can I see it again?”. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the shooter on the stand may ask to see the targets again (a presentation). The referee can repeat each target of the stand’s menu, its list of targets, up to two times. In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, there is only one showing a day: in the morning, for the first squad. After a break of more than 10 minutes, the six singles are shown again. In Compak® Sporting in line, the first shooter can see the singles before the start, and the referee shows the first target of a double before it is shot. Details: Viewing the targets.
With the squad and the trapper

Talk in the squad is short and friendly. Greet the referee and the squad at the start. Say “Well shot” after a good stand and “Bad luck” after a miss. At the end, thank the trapper and the referee. While someone is shooting, stay quiet. More customs: Sportsmanship and manners in the squad.

A protest is your right; arguing is not. Disputing a final decision after shooting has resumed, or openly making a scene about the referee’s decisions, counts as an attempt to influence the referee. The same applies when other shooters or spectators openly criticise a ruling. Penalties follow (Chapter 11 · What counts as influencing the referee, Chapter 22 · What counts as an attempt to influence).

If English is not your language, agree with your coach or interpreter beforehand on the words you need most: the call and “Protest!”. In competition an interpreter can often help you talk to the referee. The rules do not mention interpreters, so agree on it with the referee or the organiser before the round. Coaching is not allowed (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition).

notes.html: When your shooter protests, interpret the protest and the reason at once and word for word, then the referee’s decision. Add no opinion of your own.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.meaning: The call: release the target now. Say it short and clear, the same way each time.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: I think I was behind it.
phrases.meaning: You tell the coach where you think the shot went: behind the target.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.meaning: You picked up the target late; this changes the coach’s advice, so say it.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: Can I see that one again, please?
phrases.meaning: In training: ask to see the target again. In competition only where the rules allow it.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: Can you show me with your hands?
phrases.meaning: Ask the coach to show the lead or the line with a gesture; useful when words are hard.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: Sorry, could you say that again, slowly?
phrases.meaning: You did not understand the coach or the referee: ask for a slow repeat instead of guessing.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.meaning: With a raised hand, at once, on the stand: you formally disagree with the decision.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: I saw a piece come off.
phrases.meaning: The reason for your protest: a visible piece broke off, so you think it was a hit.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.meaning: A calm question when the target looked irregular or came late. Accept the answer.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.meaning: A greeting to the referee and the squad at the start of the round.

key_points.html: Tell the coach what you saw: where you picked up the target and where the shot went
Call short and clear, the same way each time: “Pull!” or “Ready!”
Disagree at once: raise a hand and say “Protest!” (Compak® Sporting: before the next shooter calls)
Calm questions are fine; arguing after the decision is an attempt to influence the referee
Greet the squad, say “well shot”, thank the trapper and the referee

quiz.q: In Sporting™ you think the referee scored your hit as a zero. When must you protest?

options.text: At the end of the round, at the card
At once, before you call the next target
After the stand, in writing to the jury

quiz.explain: Protest at once, on the stand, with a raised hand. Calling for the next target counts as accepting the last decision.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as an attempt to influence the referee?

options.text: Asking calmly: “Was that a No Bird?”
Arguing on after shooting has resumed

quiz.explain: A protest at once is your right, and calm questions are fine. Disputing a final decision after shooting resumes counts as an attempt to influence.

quiz.q: After a miss in training the coach asks “What did you see?”. What helps him most?

options.text: Your honest picture, even if unsure

quiz.explain: The coach looks for the cause of the miss, and your picture is the main clue. “I don’t know” is useful too.
